frictionVectors.title: European Diversification Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Europe continues seeking alternatives to Algerian gas, limiting Algiers' leverage over time. Algeria is responding through long-term contracts and expanded domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Morocco Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Instability along southern borders and persistent rivalry with Morocco raise security costs around energy corridors and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External Competition for Copper Routes
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is drawing strong US, European, and Gulf interest because of its access to Congolese and Zambian minerals. Angola gains bargaining power but risks becoming primarily a transit platform for external supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Dominance
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain central to offshore production and technical capacity, while declining output and debt pressures constrain Luanda's ability to capture more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Transit Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Benin's position as an outlet for Nigerien oil and regional trade is vulnerable to political disputes, border closures, and security disruptions across the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Financed Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Port, road, and energy projects rely heavily on external lenders and contractors, creating fiscal and strategic dependence despite improved logistics capacity.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers Rebalancing
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for greater domestic value capture and stronger terms from the De Beers partnership. The dispute is commercially manageable but exposes the economy's continued reliance on diamonds.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Power Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Chronic water scarcity and a constrained electricity system could slow mineral processing and new mining investment unless regional infrastructure improves.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state participation and local processing in gold, but foreign capital, contractors, and refining networks still dominate key parts of the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgent Control of Mining Zones
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and insecurity disrupt formal production, enable illicit gold flows, and reduce the state's practical control over resource-bearing territory.

frictionVectors.title: DRC border and armed-group spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability in eastern DRC and tensions involving Rwanda continue to expose Burundi to militia movements, refugee flows, and cross-border security pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector governance
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control over nickel, rare-earth, and other mineral projects, but weak infrastructure, financing needs, and opaque contracting limit bargaining power with foreign investors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dependence in ports and connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Port, digital, and transport modernization relies heavily on European, Chinese, and other external capital, creating leverage over strategic infrastructure despite strong state institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime trafficking corridor
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's position between West Africa, Europe, and the Americas makes its waters and air links important to narcotics trafficking, requiring sustained foreign security cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: Oil, gas, and mining contract dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon production and emerging mining projects depend on foreign operators and lenders, while governance weaknesses limit domestic value capture and transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The Northwest and Southwest insurgencies continue to threaten transport, agricultural output, and infrastructure, while the Chad-Cameroon pipeline remains strategically important to external energy interests.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security and mining nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel and commercial networks provide regime protection while pursuing access to gold and other minerals, reducing transparency and state control over resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-group control of territory
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks retain influence across peripheral regions and mining zones, constraining government authority and complicating roads, logistics, and formal investment.

highlights: Oil revenues underpin a fortified transition
Sahel and Sudan crises compress strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: External security and energy leverage
frictionVectors.details: The state remains dependent on foreign military, financial, and technical partners while oil production and export infrastructure are dominated by external capital and vulnerable transit routes.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover and regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war is driving refugees, arms flows, and cross-border insecurity into eastern Chad, increasing pressure on scarce public resources and narrowing the government's room for independent policy.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest France’s control of Mayotte, while migration enforcement and the island’s strategic location constrain bilateral relations.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime resource vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Limited enforcement capacity leaves fisheries and maritime zones vulnerable to outside exploitation, while infrastructure and investment remain dependent on external partners.

highlights: Critical minerals attract competing external powers

frictionVectors.title: Conflict and cross-border mineral networks
frictionVectors.details: M23 and related armed-group activity continue to challenge state control in North Kivu, with Rwanda and other regional actors implicated in contested security and mineral networks.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque strategic-minerals partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked mining interests remain central to cobalt and copper production, while Kinshasa seeks greater fiscal returns and diversification through Western and Gulf partnerships.

highlights: Oil remains the core sovereignty constraint

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: State revenues and elite power remain heavily tied to oil, exposing Brazzaville to price volatility and limiting broader domestic control over resource-led development.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and financiers retain a major role in roads, public works, and resource-linked projects, creating long-term dependence despite government efforts to diversify partners.

highlights: Cocoa and mining value capture remain contested

frictionVectors.title: Commodity-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cocoa and mining exports generate strong growth but remain exposed to foreign price-setting, processing capacity gaps, and regulatory pressure over supply-chain transparency.

frictionVectors.title: External security and infrastructure influence
frictionVectors.details: France, the United States, China, and Gulf investors compete for strategic access, while Abidjan balances security cooperation with efforts to preserve policy autonomy.

highlights: Debt and port concessions narrow autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-base concentration
frictionVectors.details: The presence of major American, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other foreign military facilities provides revenue and leverage but makes national security deeply dependent on external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: China-linked port infrastructure and debt obligations remain central to Djibouti’s economic model, while regional competition and disputes over logistics assets limit sovereign flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and Gulf investment provide liquidity but constrain policy space and increase foreign leverage over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved, keeping Egypt reliant on diplomacy and regional pressure to protect downstream water access.

frictionVectors.title: Mature oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling production and limited diversification increase dependence on foreign operators, LNG infrastructure, and volatile energy revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque external contracting
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, U.S., and other foreign commercial interests remain important to infrastructure and hydrocarbons, while weak transparency limits domestic bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline is increasingly important amid regional naval and commercial competition, exposing sovereignty to pressure from Gulf, Turkish, and Western actors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation in gold and base-metal extraction provides revenue but leaves the state vulnerable to commodity cycles and disputes over labor and control.

frictionVectors.title: Regional logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African transport corridors, energy systems, markets, and customs access, limiting independent infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: Concession-driven economy
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, textiles, and externally financed projects provide employment but leave land, water, and industrial value chains exposed to outside firms and buyers.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The GERD expands Ethiopia's control over domestic electricity generation but continues to generate strategic friction with Egypt and Sudan over dam operations and water security.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on external financing complicate Addis Ababa's control over major transport, telecom, and energy development choices.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Strategic Mining
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater local processing and state leverage over manganese and iron resources, but foreign operators and external capital remain central to production and logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors, especially for manganese, remain vulnerable to infrastructure bottlenecks and reliance on foreign firms for financing, maintenance, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Access
frictionVectors.details: The fisheries sector faces pressure from industrial fleets and weak monitoring capacity, limiting the state's ability to protect coastal resources and local livelihoods.

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia Transport Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Trade and mobility remain closely tied to Senegalese corridors and regional infrastructure, giving Dakar significant practical influence over Gambian economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Gold Mining
frictionVectors.details: 非法 small-scale mining continues to damage water systems and agricultural land while involving transnational networks, including foreign equipment suppliers and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Accra is pressing for greater domestic value addition in gold and lithium, but debt pressures and dependence on international investors constrain its negotiating room.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou rail and port system could transform Guinea's export capacity, but its financing, construction, and operations depend heavily on foreign mining consortia and external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State efforts to increase royalties and local processing face continued dependence on foreign firms for technology, logistics, and access to global aluminum markets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Cashew Buying Power
frictionVectors.details: Cashew exports dominate rural incomes, while foreign traders and processors capture much of the value through control of finance, purchasing networks, and downstream processing.

frictionVectors.title: Narco-Political Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited maritime enforcement leave the country exposed to international trafficking networks, undermining state control over ports, borders, and security policy.

frictionVectors.title: External financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and substantial Chinese and commercial debt constrain Nairobi's policy space. Public opposition remains sensitive to perceived foreign control of infrastructure and revenue streams.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu corridor security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and regional transport corridor face insecurity and uneven commercial uptake. Competition among Gulf, Chinese, and Western partners complicates Kenya's effort to retain strategic control.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but make Lesotho dependent on a larger neighbor for infrastructure, payments, and market access. Construction delays and cost disputes periodically expose this asymmetry.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and textile vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Diamond mining and garment production rely heavily on foreign capital and external market preferences. Limited domestic processing reduces Lesotho's ability to capture full value from its resources.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore production and export infrastructure remain dominated by foreign concessionaires, leaving Liberia reliant on negotiated royalties, jobs, and tax receipts. Renegotiations can improve terms but do not yet create substantial domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail access
frictionVectors.details: The use of Buchanan and other transport corridors ties mineral expansion to external operators and regional logistics networks. Weak state capacity limits Liberia's leverage over infrastructure planning and maintenance.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil assets
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security centers continue to contest access to fields, export terminals, and National Oil Corporation institutions. Production remains vulnerable to blockades and bargaining by armed groups.

frictionVectors.title: External military influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked forces, and Gulf actors retain influence through security partnerships, arms, and political networks. Their presence limits unified Libyan control over strategic infrastructure and national decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and cobalt dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Ambatovy operation gives Madagascar access to major mineral investment but leaves processing, finance, and export logistics heavily dependent on foreign partners. Commodity-price volatility and operational problems can sharply affect national revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Ilmenite and land tensions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mineral sands operations have generated disputes over land, compensation, and environmental impacts. Foreign ownership and limited local value addition continue to fuel concerns about sovereignty over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-supported reforms limit policy freedom while restoring access to financing. Currency and import pressures continue to affect sovereign control over essential goods.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and power bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium and rare-earth projects attract foreign capital, but weak electricity, rail, and processing capacity could leave Malawi primarily an ore exporter.

highlights: Junta tightens control over strategic mining
Russian security ties replace Western leverage

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking a larger state share of gold revenues and stronger local processing, increasing tensions with international operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Security and logistics isolation
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security support and strained relations with Western partners complicate access to finance, technology, and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led energy development
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project and proposed hydrogen investments can expand state revenues, but financing, technology, and export infrastructure remain externally controlled.

frictionVectors.title: Resource governance and inclusion
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gas, and future hydrogen projects raise concerns over revenue distribution, labor inclusion, and the risk of enclave-style development.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty and maritime access
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved Chagos settlement and the Diego Garcia military facility remain central constraints on Mauritius's full control of its maritime territory and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External capital concentration
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, finance, and port activity depend on international investors and external demand, creating exposure without amounting to direct resource capture.

highlights: Renewables and phosphates anchor strategic autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy security
frictionVectors.details: Drought and rising demand increase dependence on desalination, imported energy, and large infrastructure suppliers despite strong renewable investment.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries, and renewable projects in Western Sahara generate economic leverage but remain exposed to legal challenges and diplomatic disputes over sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign LNG Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique relies on international energy companies, lenders, and export infrastructure to monetize its gas reserves. Delays, cost overruns, and security risks limit the state’s bargaining power and domestic benefit.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence continues to threaten communities, logistics corridors, and offshore-linked projects. External military and security support remains important to protecting strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-Mineral Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms are competing for uranium, lithium, rare earths, and other mineral opportunities. Namibia is seeking greater local processing and state participation but still depends heavily on external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrogen Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large green-hydrogen ambitions require foreign finance, export agreements, and port infrastructure. The main sovereignty risk is that projects could export low-value energy while leaving Namibia with limited industrial spillovers.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The military government is renegotiating or challenging longstanding Western-linked mining arrangements while seeking alternative partners. This may increase state control but also raises risks of production disruption, legal disputes, and opaque concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Security-Partner Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces has increased reliance on regional allies and Russian-linked security support. Sovereignty gains are constrained by persistent jihadist violence and dependence on external military capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria is trying to attract international investment while retaining greater national value from oil and gas. Production losses, contract uncertainty, and dependence on foreign technology continue to weaken sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Infrastructure Fragility
frictionVectors.details: Pipeline theft, sabotage, gas-supply constraints, and chronic grid weakness limit domestic energy security. Imported fuel and externally financed infrastructure expose the economy to price, credit, and geopolitical shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda remains an important trading and processing hub for Great Lakes minerals, attracting external buyers and scrutiny over supply-chain traceability. International pressure could constrain the state’s commercial flexibility and reputation.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Accusations of support for armed actors in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to generate diplomatic and sanctions risk. Regional insecurity threatens trade corridors and complicates Rwanda’s infrastructure and investment partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Exploration
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe is seeking offshore petroleum investment, but commercial discoveries and meaningful state revenue remain uncertain. Licensing decisions could create future sovereignty and transparency pressures.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago relies heavily on foreign financing and technical assistance for ports, energy, and maritime surveillance. Competition among European, Chinese, and other partners gives the government leverage but limits strategic autonomy.

highlights: New oil and gas era begins

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater national participation and fiscal returns from offshore projects involving foreign operators. Aggressive renegotiation could improve sovereignty but risks litigation, investment delays, and strained relations with partners.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and Coastal Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing agreements and offshore energy development are intensifying competition over Senegal's coastal resources. Local fishing communities remain vulnerable to reduced access, pollution risks, and opaque licensing.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles is balancing security and infrastructure ties with India, China, France, and other partners. Port, airport, and maritime-surveillance cooperation can strengthen sovereignty while raising concerns about strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Ocean Resource Governance
frictionVectors.details: The country's blue-bond and marine-conservation model offers greater control over ocean assets, but enforcement capacity remains limited. Foreign fishing activity, shipping, and climate damage continue to pressure fisheries and maritime revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Mineral Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile, and other mining projects are central to growth but leave Sierra Leone exposed to foreign capital, commodity cycles, and uneven revenue capture. Contract transparency, environmental safeguards, and local processing remain major sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining logistics depend on foreign-backed port, rail, and road infrastructure. These arrangements can unlock exports while concentrating strategic control over transport corridors in external operators and financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil and Licensing
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is promoting offshore petroleum licensing amid disputes over federal and state authority, limited regulatory capacity, and insecurity. Foreign operators and advisers are gaining access before the country has fully consolidated transparent revenue-sharing institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Security Patrons
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, the United States, and regional actors support different security and infrastructure relationships. These partnerships help counter al-Shabaab and protect maritime routes but can deepen federal fragmentation and external leverage over ports and resources.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and critical-minerals control
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation and supply-chain control, but foreign capital, electricity constraints, and regulatory uncertainty limit its leverage over platinum-group metals, manganese, and other strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and freight infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability has improved from crisis levels but remains vulnerable, while rail and port congestion continues to constrain mineral exports and national economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on pipelines and export infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving oil revenues exposed to conflict, transit disruption, and bargaining pressure from external operators and neighboring states.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and external resource capture
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and weak institutions allow oil, gold, and humanitarian supply chains to be captured by armed and commercial networks, limiting broad national control over resources.

highlights: Gold and corridors drive external competition

frictionVectors.title: Gold economy and foreign patrons
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed authorities rely on gold and cross-border commercial networks, while outside sponsors seek influence over extraction, finance, and strategic territory.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, pipelines, and aid access
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, oil transit routes, and humanitarian corridors is contested, allowing military actors and foreign partners to convert infrastructure access into political leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and gas contract leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for greater state participation, local processing, and revenue capture in gold, graphite, nickel, and natural gas, but still depends on foreign capital and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and regional corridors
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of Dar es Salaam-linked rail and port infrastructure strengthens Tanzania's regional position, while competition among Gulf, Chinese, and Western partners creates persistent influence risks.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major regional transshipment and trade hub, but its financing, logistics, and security ecosystem leaves Togo exposed to competing external commercial and political interests.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and instability moving south from the Sahel threaten northern border communities and could increase reliance on foreign security assistance and surveillance infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European support for border control and macroeconomic assistance gives Brussels substantial leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic resistance is growing against arrangements perceived as outsourcing migration enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and phosphate vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains exposed to imported energy and declining phosphate-sector performance, limiting its bargaining power with foreign lenders and investors.

highlights: Oil corridor advances under external pressure

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline is strengthening Kampala's future export position, but Western criticism, financing constraints, and environmental disputes continue to raise project costs and diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and Gulf-linked capital supports transport and energy projects, while debt-servicing pressures constrain Uganda's ability to retain full strategic control over infrastructure assets.

highlights: Debt restructuring restores room to maneuver

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using renewed interest from the United States, Europe, China, and Gulf investors to diversify copper partnerships, but ownership, processing, and revenue-sharing terms remain contested.

frictionVectors.title: Transport corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper exports rely on vulnerable regional rail and road corridors, particularly through Tanzania and neighboring southern African states, leaving Zambia exposed to logistical and political bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe is restricting unprocessed lithium exports to promote domestic value addition, yet limited capital, technology, and power supply preserve substantial leverage for Chinese and other foreign mining firms.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and sanctions constraints
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, sanctions-related financial isolation, and electricity shortages reduce the state's ability to capture stable mineral revenues or independently finance processing infrastructure.
